claim: Neural selectivity to orientation is one of the simplest and most thoroughly-studied cortical sensory features.
source: Neural selectivity to orientation is one of the simplest and most thoroughly-studied cortical sensory features.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Stimulus vignetting can wholly determine the orientation selectivity of responses in visual cortex measured at a macroscopic scale.
source: Our results demonstrate that stimulus vignetting can wholly determine the orientation selectivity of responses in visual cortex measured at a macroscopic scale, and suggest a reinterpretation of a well-established literature on orientation processing in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data and model simulations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Primary visual cortex (V1) is likely the best studied sensory cortical area.
source: Primary visual cortex (V1) is likely the best studied sensory cortical area, and is a model for understanding broad principles of cortical processing.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Orientation in V1 is one of the simplest and best studied cortical sensory features.
source: Orientation in V1 is one of the simplest and best studied cortical sensory features.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Oriented V1-like receptive fields play an important role in successful computational models of vision.
source: Orientation is used as a model for understanding more complex feature processing in other cortical areas, and oriented V1-like receptive fields play an important role in successful computational models of vision.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The map of orientation in V1 is inadequately understood.
source: Yet the map of orientation in V1 is inadequately understood.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their interpretation of the literature.

claim: At a fine scale, the orientation map shows an orderly periodic structure with pinwheels in hypercolumns.
source: At a fine scale, the map shows an orderly periodic structure with pinwheels in hypercolumns, which have a periodicity of about 1 mm in monkeys (Hubel and Wiesel, 1963; Blasdel and Salama, 1986; Grinvald et al., 1986; Das and Gilbert, 1997; Maldonado et al., 1997; Ohki et al., 2006), and about 2 mm in humans (Adams et al., 2007; Yacoub et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hypercolumns have a periodicity of about 1 mm in monkeys.
source: At a fine scale, the map shows an orderly periodic structure with pinwheels in hypercolumns, which have a periodicity of about 1 mm in monkeys (Hubel and Wiesel, 1963; Blasdel and Salama, 1986; Grinvald et al., 1986; Das and Gilbert, 1997; Maldonado et al., 1997; Ohki et al., 2006), and about 2 mm in humans (Adams et al., 2007; Yacoub et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on monkey V1.

claim: Hypercolumns have a periodicity of about 2 mm in humans.
source: At a fine scale, the map shows an orderly periodic structure with pinwheels in hypercolumns, which have a periodicity of about 1 mm in monkeys (Hubel and Wiesel, 1963; Blasdel and Salama, 1986; Grinvald et al., 1986; Das and Gilbert, 1997; Maldonado et al., 1997; Ohki et al., 2006), and about 2 mm in humans (Adams et al., 2007; Yacoub et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on human V1.

claim: The coarse-scale structure of orientation selectivity is poorly established.
source: While the fine-scale structure has been studied extensively, the coarse-scale structure of orientation selectivity is poorly established.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their interpretation of the literature.

claim: Using fMRI, researchers have described a coarse-scale orientation bias in human V1.
source: We and others, using fMRI, have described a coarse-scale orientation bias in human V1; each voxel exhibits an orientation preference that depends on the region of space that it represents (Furmanski and Engel, 2000; Sasaki et al., 2006; Mannion et al., 2010; Freeman et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2013; Larsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior fMRI research.

claim: Each voxel exhibits an orientation preference that depends on the region of space that it represents.
source: We and others, using fMRI, have described a coarse-scale orientation bias in human V1; each voxel exhibits an orientation preference that depends on the region of space that it represents (Furmanski and Engel, 2000; Sasaki et al., 2006; Mannion et al., 2010; Freeman et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2013; Larsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior fMRI research.

claim: A radial bias is observed most clearly in the peripheral representation of V1.
source: We observed a radial bias most clearly in the peripheral representation of V1: voxels that responded to peripheral locations near the vertical meridian tended to respond most strongly to vertical orientations; voxels along the peripheral horizontal meridian responded most strongly to horizontal orientations; likewise for oblique orientations.
evidence: This is a description of the authors' prior observations.

claim: Voxels that responded to peripheral locations near the vertical meridian tended to respond most strongly to vertical orientations.
source: We observed a radial bias most clearly in the peripheral representation of V1: voxels that responded to peripheral locations near the vertical meridian tended to respond most strongly to vertical orientations; voxels along the peripheral horizontal meridian responded most strongly to horizontal orientations; likewise for oblique orientations.
evidence: This is a description of the authors' prior observations.

claim: Voxels along the peripheral horizontal meridian responded most strongly to horizontal orientations.
source: We observed a radial bias most clearly in the peripheral representation of V1: voxels that responded to peripheral locations near the vertical meridian tended to respond most strongly to vertical orientations; voxels along the peripheral horizontal meridian responded most strongly to horizontal orientations; likewise for oblique orientations.
evidence: This is a description of the authors' prior observations.

claim: This phenomenon had gone mostly unnoticed in single-unit recording studies.
source: This phenomenon had gone mostly unnoticed in single-unit recording studies.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their review of the literature.

claim: fMRI is well-suited to measuring coarse-scale orientation biases because fMRI covers the entire retinotopic map in visual cortex.
source: fMRI is well-suited to measuring coarse-scale orientation biases because fMRI covers the entire retinotopic map in visual cortex.
evidence: This is an assertion based on the properties of fMRI as a measurement technique.

claim: A number of previous studies have asserted that orientation preferences in fMRI measurements arise primarily from random spatial irregularities in the fine-scale columnar architecture.
source: A number of previous studies have asserted that orientation preferences in fMRI measurements arise primarily from random spatial irregularities in the fine-scale columnar architecture (Boynton, 2005; Haynes and Rees, 2005; Kamitani and Tong, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This conjecture has inspired a large literature on the use of multivariate statistical analyses to exploit these small biases.
source: This conjecture has inspired a large literature on the use of multivariate statistical analyses to exploit these small biases, both to study orientation selectivity in V1 and to study a wide range of other functions throughout the brain.
evidence: This is an assertion about the impact of prior research on the field.

claim: The authors have argued that the coarse-scale orientation bias is the predominant orientation-selective signal measured with fMRI.
source: On the other hand, we have argued that the coarse-scale orientation bias is the predominant orientation-selective signal measured with fMRI, and that multivariate decoding analysis methods are successful because of it (Freeman et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: Multivariate decoding analysis methods are successful because of the coarse-scale orientation bias.
source: On the other hand, we have argued that the coarse-scale orientation bias is the predominant orientation-selective signal measured with fMRI, and that multivariate decoding analysis methods are successful because of it (Freeman et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: The relative contribution of coarse- and fine-scale biases remains hotly debated.
source: The relative contribution of coarse- and fine-scale biases remains hotly debated (Pratte et al., 2016; Alink et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research papers.

claim: The neural basis for the coarse-scale orientation bias is unknown.
source: Second, while the neural architecture that gives rise to orientation selectivity is well understood, the neural basis for the coarse-scale orientation bias is unknown.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Carlson (2014) proposed that the coarse-scale bias is a byproduct of the edge of the stimulus, referring to it as an 'edge effect.'
source: Carlson (2014) proposed that the coarse-scale bias is a byproduct of the edge of the stimulus, referring to it as an 'edge effect.'
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carlson (2014).

claim: By Carlson's account, the coarse-scale bias does not directly reflect enhanced neural responses for particular orientations, but rather arises from properties of the stimulus.
source: By this account, the coarse-scale bias does not directly reflect enhanced neural responses for particular orientations, but rather arises from properties of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of Carlson's (2014) proposal.

claim: The vignette spreads Fourier energy.
source: The principle underlying stimulus vignetting is that the vignette spreads Fourier energy.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle stated by the authors.

claim: The direction and amplitude of Fourier energy spread is determined by the underlying stimulus spectrum and the aperture geometry.
source: The direction and amplitude of this spread is determined by the underlying stimulus spectrum and the aperture geometry, in much the same way that the Fourier transform of a sinusoid windowed by a rectangle consists of the sinusoid frequency convolved with a sinc function.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle stated by the authors, drawing on established Fourier analysis.

claim: Due to spectral spread at the aperture edge, neurons with receptive fields straddling the aperture edge respond to a combination of spatial frequency and orientation components, different from neurons with receptive fields far from the edge.
source: Due to this spectral spread at the aperture edge, neurons with receptive fields straddling the aperture edge respond to a combination of spatial frequency and orientation components, different from neurons with receptive fields far from the edge (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the Fourier analysis principle, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The computational model simulated the results of Freeman et al. (2011) fMRI experiment.
source: We began by simulating the results of our previous fMRI experiment (Freeman et al., 2011) with an image-computable model of V1 (Simoncelli et al., 1992) (see Materials and methods: Theoretical Model).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The inputs to the model were identical to the stimuli used by Freeman et al. (2011).
source: The inputs to the model were identical to the stimuli used by Freeman et al. (2011).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: The stimuli consisted of 16 evenly spaced orientation angles between 0° and 180°.
source: Specifically, the stimuli consisted of 16 evenly spaced orientation angles between 0° and 180°.
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli used in the simulation.

claim: All stimuli were vignetted by a 4° annulus (inner radius, 5°; outer radius, 9°).
source: All stimuli were vignetted by a 4° annulus (inner radius, 5°; outer radius, 9°).
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli used in the simulation.

claim: Both the inner and outer edges of the annulus were blurred with a 1° raised-cosine transition.
source: Both the inner and outer edges of the annulus were blurred with a 1° raised-cosine transition (centered on the inner and outer edges).
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli used in the simulation.

claim: The model's responses were measured to each image separately.
source: We measured the model's responses to each image separately.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling procedure.

claim: Each pixel of the model's output can be thought of as a simulated neuron in the retinotopic map of V1.
source: Each pixel of the model's output can be thought of as a simulated neuron in the retinotopic map of V1.
evidence: This is an explanation of how to interpret the model output.

claim: To simulate an fMRI voxel's response, the model responses were summed across all orientation channels.
source: To simulate an fMRI voxel's response to the stimuli used in Freeman et al., we summed the model responses across all orientation channels.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling procedure.

claim: The simulated fMRI responses exhibit a clear coarse-scale bias for orientation.
source: But the simulated fMRI responses do in fact exhibit a clear coarse-scale bias for orientation (Figure 2), replicating previous results (Carlson, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulation, shown in Figure 2 and supported by citation to Carlson (2014).

claim: The coarse-scale orientation bias matched Freeman et al. (2011) in that the largest responses were observed for radial orientations.
source: The coarse-scale orientation bias matched Freeman et al. (2011) in that the largest responses were observed for radial orientations (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulation, shown in Figure 2 and compared to prior empirical results.

claim: Orientation-selective responses measured with fMRI could reflect, at least in part, the shape of the vignette, rather than the underlying orientation tuning of individual neurons.
source: The simulation results suggest that orientation-selective responses measured with fMRI could reflect, at least in part, the shape of the vignette, rather than the underlying orientation tuning of individual neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: If the vignette affects orientation bias, changing the vignette should have a predictable effect on orientation bias.
source: To test this possibility, we generated a novel set of stimuli with vignettes that were orthogonal to one another. If the vignette affects orientation bias, changing the vignette should have a predictable effect on orientation bias.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: The novel stimuli were created by multiplying vertical and horizontal Cartesian gratings (the carrier) by a radial or an angular polar grating (the modulator).
source: The novel stimuli for this simulation were created as follows. Vertical and horizontal Cartesian gratings (the carrier) were multiplied by a radial or an angular polar grating (the modulator).
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli used in the simulation.

claim: The model predicted that the coarse-scale orientation bias should depend on the modulator.
source: The model predicted that the coarse-scale orientation bias should depend on the modulator.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The radial modulator evoked a coarse-scale bias that was radial.
source: The radial modulator evoked a coarse-scale bias that was radial (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulation, shown in Figure 3.

claim: At regions around the vertical meridian there is a greater response for the vertical orientation than for the horizontal orientation.
source: In other words, at regions around the vertical meridian there is a greater response for the vertical orientation than for the horizontal orientation (light regions in Figure 3), and vice versa around the horizontal meridian (dark regions in Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulation, shown in Figure 3.

claim: The model predicted that changing the orientation of the modulator should affect the orientation preference to the carrier grating.
source: The model predicted that changing the orientation of the modulator should affect the orientation preference to the carrier grating.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The angular modulator evoked a coarse-scale bias that was tangential.
source: We found that the angular modulator evoked a coarse-scale bias that was tangential.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulation.

claim: At the vertical meridian the horizontal grating yielded higher energy, and at the horizontal meridian the vertical grating evokes higher energy responses.
source: Thus, at the vertical meridian the horizontal grating yielded higher energy, and at the horizontal meridian the vertical grating evokes higher energy responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulation.

claim: The stimuli used in Freeman et al. (2011) had vignettes with gradual contrast changes.
source: The stimuli used in Freeman et al. (2011), and in our simulations in Figure 2, had vignettes with gradual contrast changes, indicating that the impact of vignetting on orientation bias is not dependent on the presence of sharp edges.
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli used in prior work and the current simulations.

claim: The impact of vignetting on orientation bias is not dependent on the presence of sharp edges.
source: The stimuli used in Freeman et al. (2011), and in our simulations in Figure 2, had vignettes with gradual contrast changes, indicating that the impact of vignetting on orientation bias is not dependent on the presence of sharp edges.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stimuli characteristics.

claim: Similar results were found for both sinusoidal modulators and modulators with hard edges.
source: We found similar results for both sinusoidal modulators and modulators with hard edges (i.e. square-wave), as expected, because vignetting arises from any contrast change in the image, rather than an 'edge' per se (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Vignetting arises from any contrast change in the image, rather than an 'edge' per se.
source: We found similar results for both sinusoidal modulators and modulators with hard edges (i.e. square-wave), as expected, because vignetting arises from any contrast change in the image, rather than an 'edge' per se (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an explanation of the theoretical basis for the findings.

claim: Evidence of stimulus vignetting was found at both 3T and 7T field strengths.
source: We found evidence of stimulus vignetting at both 3T and 7T field strengths, at different spatial resolutions, and for both square wave and sinusoidal modulators, as predicted by the theoretical model.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI experimental findings.

claim: Evidence of stimulus vignetting was found at different spatial resolutions.
source: We found evidence of stimulus vignetting at both 3T and 7T field strengths, at different spatial resolutions, and for both square wave and sinusoidal modulators, as predicted by the theoretical model.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI experimental findings.

claim: Evidence of stimulus vignetting was found for both square wave and sinusoidal modulators.
source: We found evidence of stimulus vignetting at both 3T and 7T field strengths, at different spatial resolutions, and for both square wave and sinusoidal modulators, as predicted by the theoretical model.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI experimental findings.

claim: The radial modulator evoked a radial bias in fMRI experiments.
source: The radial modulator evoked a radial bias, that is, orientation preferences pointing inward toward the fovea (Figure 4, top row).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The angular modulator evoked a tangential bias in fMRI experiments.
source: The angular modulator evoked a tangential bias, that is, orientation preferences that were rotated by 90 deg from radial (Figure 4, bottom row).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments, shown in Figure 4.

claim: On a voxel-by-voxel basis, preferred orientations were shifted by 90 deg across modulators.
source: Furthermore, on a voxel-by-voxel basis, preferred orientations were shifted by 90 deg across modulators (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments, shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is a clear correspondence between predicted and measured orientation preference.
source: Comparing model predictions to data from individual voxels, we observed a clear correspondence between predicted and measured orientation preference (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model predictions to fMRI data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Circular correlations between predicted and measured orientation preferences were 0.26 and 0.20 for radial and angular modulators, respectively (p<0.0001 for both).
source: Circular correlations between predicted and measured orientation preferences were 0.26 and 0.20 for radial and angular modulators, respectively (p<0.0001 for both).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing model predictions to fMRI data.

claim: Within-modulator decoding yielded high accuracies (p<0.001).
source: Within-modulator decoding yielded high accuracies (Figure 7A, left, p<0.001, tested with a non-parametric permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI decoding analysis, shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Across-modulator decoding accuracy was below chance (p<0.0001).
source: Across-modulator decoding accuracy was below chance (Figure 7A, middle, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI decoding analysis, shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The population response to oriented gratings was dependent on the modulator.
source: These results indicate that the population response to oriented gratings was dependent on the modulator — responses to an oriented grating multiplied by one modulator (e.g. radial) were entirely different from responses to the same oriented grating when multiplied by the other modulator (e.g., by the angular modulator).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decoding results.

claim: After shifting the orientation labels by 90°, decoding accuracy returned to levels significantly above chance (p<0.0001).
source: After shifting the orientation labels, decoding accuracy returned to levels significantly above chance (Figure 7A, right, p<0.0001), only slightly lower than within-modulator decoding accuracy on the unshifted data.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI decoding analysis, shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The difference between within-modulator decoding accuracy and between-modulator decoding accuracy after shifting labels was small but statistically significant (p=0.046).
source: The difference between within-modulator decoding accuracy and between-modulator decoding accuracy after shifting labels was small but statistically significant (p=0.046).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI decoding analysis.

claim: Stimulus vignetting strongly affects voxel orientation bias.
source: Our results show that stimulus vignetting strongly affects voxel orientation bias.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Results from many fMRI studies attempting to measure neural orientation tuning properties may actually reflect stimulus vignetting.
source: This suggests that results from many fMRI studies attempting to measure neural orientation tuning properties may actually reflect stimulus vignetting.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Stimulus vignetting masquerades as orientation selectivity amongst voxels that correspond to the stimulus edge.
source: Since stimulus vignetting masquerades as orientation selectivity amongst voxels that correspond to the stimulus edge, and because edges tend to be continuous over a large spatial extent, vignetting will generally result in a coarse-scale map of orientation bias.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and theoretical understanding.

claim: Edges tend to be continuous over a large spatial extent.
source: Since stimulus vignetting masquerades as orientation selectivity amongst voxels that correspond to the stimulus edge, and because edges tend to be continuous over a large spatial extent, vignetting will generally result in a coarse-scale map of orientation bias.
evidence: This is a general observation about stimulus properties.

claim: Vignetting will generally result in a coarse-scale map of orientation bias.
source: Since stimulus vignetting masquerades as orientation selectivity amongst voxels that correspond to the stimulus edge, and because edges tend to be continuous over a large spatial extent, vignetting will generally result in a coarse-scale map of orientation bias.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and theoretical understanding.

claim: In many fMRI studies, gratings are presented within a circular annulus.
source: In many fMRI studies, gratings are presented within a circular annulus (Haynes and Rees, 2005; Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Freeman et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2013; Larsson et al., 2017; Wardle et al., 2017), and in these cases the model predicts a radial coarse-scale bias.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: When gratings are presented within a circular annulus, the model predicts a radial coarse-scale bias.
source: In many fMRI studies, gratings are presented within a circular annulus (Haynes and Rees, 2005; Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Freeman et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2013; Larsson et al., 2017; Wardle et al., 2017), and in these cases the model predicts a radial coarse-scale bias.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model applied to common experimental designs.

claim: In some cases, other stimulus vignetting exists, resulting in more subtle coarse-scale patterns of orientation bias.
source: However, in some cases, other stimulus vignetting exists, resulting in more subtle coarse-scale patterns of orientation bias (Swisher et al., 2010; Larsson et al., 2017; Sengupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: One study (Alink et al., 2017) used inner and outer circular annuli, but added additional angular edges.
source: One study (Alink et al., 2017) used inner and outer circular annuli, but added additional angular edges, the result of which should be a combination of radial and tangential biases.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus design in a prior study.

claim: The result of using inner and outer circular annuli with additional angular edges should be a combination of radial and tangential biases.
source: One study (Alink et al., 2017) used inner and outer circular annuli, but added additional angular edges, the result of which should be a combination of radial and tangential biases.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model applied to a specific experimental design.

claim: Alink et al. (2017) reported that voxels had a mixed pattern of selectivity, with a considerable number of voxels reliably preferring tangential gratings, and other voxels reliably favoring radial orientations.
source: Indeed, this study reported that voxels had a mixed pattern of selectivity, with a considerable number of voxels reliably preferring tangential gratings, and other voxels reliably favoring radial orientations.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: Stimulus vignetting is a general issue of concern in visual neuroscience.
source: Stimulus vignetting is a general issue of concern in visual neuroscience (Carter and Henning, 1971; Larsson et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Whenever a neuron's receptive field overlaps a stimulus edge or a change in contrast, stimulus vignetting will spread the Fourier power and affect the neuron's response.
source: According to the theoretical framework that we have applied here, whenever a neuron's receptive field overlaps a stimulus edge or a change in contrast, stimulus vignetting will spread the Fourier power and affect the neuron's response.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: A neuron may exhibit ostensible orientation tuning even when it is not orientation selective.
source: As a result, such a neuron may exhibit ostensible orientation tuning even when it is not orientation selective.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: Even if a neuron is truly orientation selective, measurements of its orientation tuning may be confounded by the aperture shape.
source: Furthermore, even if a neuron is truly orientation selective, measurements of its orientation tuning may be confounded by the aperture shape.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: Vignetting may produce ostensible selectivity to second-order features, including vignettes themselves.
source: Vignetting may produce ostensible selectivity to second-order features, including vignettes themselves.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: A V1 neuron with a receptive field near the vertical meridian might respond more to a radial modulated vertical grating than to an angular modulated vertical grating simply as a result of vignetting.
source: For example, consider the modulated gratings that we used in the current study. A V1 neuron with a receptive field near the vertical meridian (i.e., near the V1/V2 border) might respond more to a radial modulated vertical grating than to an angular modulated vertical grating simply as a result of vignetting.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: This could be misinterpreted as sensitivity to second-order orientation contrast.
source: This could be misinterpreted as sensitivity to second-order orientation contrast (Zhou and Baker, 1993; Mareschal and Baker, 1998; Song and Baker, 2007), when in fact the neuron is sensitive only to first-order orientation.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study, with citations to prior work on second-order orientation contrast.

claim: There are no so-called 'second-order filters' in the model.
source: There are no so-called 'second-order filters' in our model.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The model exhibits orientation-selective biases for 2nd-order modulation because of vignetting.
source: Yet it exhibits orientation-selective biases for 2nd-order modulation because of vignetting.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Vignetting might account for ostensible selectivity to orientation of illusory contours and second-order patterns, in both single-cell and fMRI studies.
source: Similarly, vignetting might account for ostensible selectivity to orientation of illusory contours and second-order patterns, in both single-cell (Grosof et al., 1993) and fMRI studies (Larsson et al., 2006; Montaser-Kouhsari et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study, with citations to prior research.

claim: Vignetting may even produce ostensible orientation selectivity in neurons that are not orientation selective at all.
source: Vignetting may even produce ostensible orientation selectivity in neurons that are not orientation selective at all.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: A major question concerning the neural origin of orientation selectivity is whether and to what degree lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) responses are tuned to orientation.
source: A major question concerning the neural origin of orientation selectivity is whether and to what degree lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) responses are tuned to orientation (Ling et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of an open question in the field, supported by citations.

claim: One group found that orientation can be decoded from LGN, suggesting that thalamic responses are tuned to orientation.
source: Recently, one group addressed this question using fMRI. They found that orientation can be decoded from LGN, suggesting that thalamic responses are tuned to orientation (Ling et al., 2015), perhaps inheriting their selectivity from the retina (Schall et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: Another group, using calcium imaging to measure bouton responses in mice, found extensive orientation tuning.
source: Another group, using calcium imaging to measure bouton responses in mice, found extensive orientation tuning as well (Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: Stimulus vignetting may have played a critical role in both of these studies.
source: But stimulus vignetting may have played a critical role in both of these studies.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors about the interpretation of prior studies.

claim: In Ling et al. (2015), gratings were presented within a circular annulus, likely yielding a radial bias due to stimulus vignetting.
source: In the former study (Ling et al., 2015), gratings were presented within a circular annulus, likely yielding a radial bias due to stimulus vignetting.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors about the interpretation of a prior study.

claim: In Sun et al. (2016), the grating covered the entire visual display (75 deg x 75 deg), which is nearly the entire extent of the mouse monocular visual field.
source: In the latter study (Sun et al., 2016), the grating covered the entire visual display (75 deg x 75 deg), which is nearly the entire extent of the mouse monocular visual field.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus design in a prior study.

claim: Mouse neuronal receptive fields are large, at least an order of magnitude larger than in primates.
source: However, mouse neuronal receptive fields are large, at least an order of magnitude larger than in primates (Van den Bergh et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A significant portion of neurons recorded by Sun et al. (2016) may have had receptive fields that overlapped the edges of the screen, which would have resulted in vignetting.
source: A significant portion of neurons recorded by Sun et al. (2016) may have therefore had receptive fields that overlapped the edges of the screen, which would have resulted in vignetting.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors about the interpretation of a prior study.

claim: These and many other related studies may not have been measuring orientation selectivity at all, but rather activity reflecting stimulus vignetting.
source: These and many other related studies may not have been measuring orientation selectivity at all, but rather activity reflecting stimulus vignetting.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors about the interpretation of prior studies.

claim: The authors found no evidence for any other orientation information present in the data.
source: Do voxel responses contain any orientation preferences that are not the result of stimulus vignetting? We found no evidence for any other orientation information present in the data.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings from the current study.

claim: Based on the current study, the authors cannot rule out the possibility of other factors affecting fMRI orientation preferences, at both coarse and fine spatial scales.
source: Based on the current study we cannot rule out the possibility of other factors affecting fMRI orientation preferences, at both coarse and fine spatial scales.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: Fine-scale signals originating from a columnar organization may, theoretically, affect fMRI signals.
source: For example, fine-scale signals originating from a columnar organization may, theoretically, affect fMRI signals (Boynton, 2005).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility acknowledged by the authors, with a citation.

claim: These columnar signals may be entirely eclipsed by stimulus vignetting.
source: But these columnar signals may be entirely eclipsed by stimulus vignetting.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors.

claim: Coarse-scale signals such as a physiological radial bias may indeed exist, but be relatively small, and hence also eclipsed by stimulus vignetting.
source: Similarly, coarse-scale signals such as a physiological radial bias may indeed exist, but be relatively small, and hence also eclipsed by stimulus vignetting.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors.

claim: The authors' previous results, describing a vertical bias near the fovea, in addition to the radial bias in the periphery, lend support to the possibility that there are multiple sources of coarse-scale bias.
source: Our previous results, describing a vertical bias near the fovea (Freeman et al., 2013), in addition to the radial bias in the periphery (Freeman et al., 2011), lend support to the possibility that there are multiple sources of coarse-scale bias.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the authors' prior work, supported by citations.

claim: If each voxel reflects the activity of a large number of neurons, signals from multiple orientation columns will be summed within a voxel, thus attenuating any columnar signal.
source: Do fMRI voxels reflect any fine-scale orientation signals originating from a columnar organization, in addition to an orientation bias resulting from vignetting? If each voxel reflects the activity of a large number of neurons, signals from multiple orientation columns will be summed within a voxel, thus attenuating any columnar signal.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of fMRI.

claim: If this is the case, decreasing the voxel size should lower the number of different columns summed within each voxel, and amplify columnar orientation selectivity.
source: If this is the case, decreasing the voxel size should lower the number of different columns summed within each voxel, and amplify columnar orientation selectivity.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of fMRI.

claim: Orientation bias resulting from vignetting should not depend on scanning resolution.
source: On the other hand, orientation bias resulting from vignetting should not depend on scanning resolution.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: Nearby neurons respond to nearby locations in the visual field, and therefore will respond similarly to the vignette.
source: Nearby neurons respond to nearby locations in the visual field, and therefore will respond similarly to the vignette.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of visual cortex organization.

claim: Increasing the acquisition resolution will augment columnar signals but not vignetting signals.
source: Thus, increasing the acquisition resolution will augment columnar signals but not vignetting signals.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the framework presented in the study.

claim: The authors' results at 2 mm voxels demonstrate primarily vignetting with no evidence of a columnar signal.
source: Our results at 2 mm voxels demonstrate primarily vignetting with no evidence of a columnar signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments.

claim: Increasing the acquisition resolution to 0.9 mm did not alter this result.
source: Increasing the acquisition resolution to 0.9 mm did not alter this result.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments.

claim: The coarse-scale bias due to vignetting is the predominant source of orientation information measured with fMRI at scanning resolutions with voxel sizes of 1 mm or larger.
source: From this we conclude that the coarse-scale bias due to vignetting is the predominant source of orientation information measured with fMRI at scanning resolutions with voxel sizes of 1 mm or larger.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The authors are no longer arguing about whether orientation decoding is dominated by coarse-scale orientation biases; they already know that it is.
source: We are no longer arguing about whether orientation decoding is dominated by coarse-scale orientation biases; we already know that it is.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' position based on their prior work.

claim: An extreme method the authors previously used for testing whether fine-scale information contributes to fMRI orientation decoding involved shifting the acquired slices by half a voxel (1 mm), and then attempting to decode the grating orientation.
source: An extreme method we previously used for testing whether fine-scale information contributes to fMRI orientation decoding involved shifting the acquired slices by half a voxel (1 mm), and then attempting to decode the grating orientation (Freeman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of a method used in the authors' prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: If successful decoding depends on fine-scale information, shifting the slices should eradicate any decoding information.
source: If successful decoding depends on fine-scale information, shifting the slices should eradicate any decoding information.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of fine-scale information.

claim: Decoding accuracy was unaffected (statistically indistinguishable) by shifting the slices.
source: In fact, decoding accuracy was unaffected (statistically indistinguishable) by shifting the slices.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' prior work.

claim: The finding that a coarse-scale bias is the source of orientation decoding remains controversial.
source: However, the finding that a coarse-scale bias is the source of orientation decoding remains controversial, and several recent studies have attempted to disprove it (Alink et al., 2013; Pratte et al., 2016; Alink et al., 2017), in part, we believe, because the notion that fMRI is sensitive to fine-scale neural activity is highly attractive.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the field, supported by citations.

claim: Several recent studies have attempted to disprove the finding that a coarse-scale bias is the source of orientation decoding.
source: However, the finding that a coarse-scale bias is the source of orientation decoding remains controversial, and several recent studies have attempted to disprove it (Alink et al., 2013; Pratte et al., 2016; Alink et al., 2017), in part, we believe, because the notion that fMRI is sensitive to fine-scale neural activity is highly attractive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research papers.

claim: The authors have no doubt that there are orientation columns in human V1.
source: We have no doubt that there are orientation columns in human V1.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' belief based on established knowledge.

claim: The authors have no doubt that orientation-decoding with fMRI at conventional resolutions is dominated by coarse-scale orientation bias, not the fine-scale (columnar) architecture for orientation selectivity.
source: But we also have no doubt that orientation-decoding with fMRI at conventional resolutions is dominated by coarse-scale orientation bias, not the fine-scale (columnar) architecture for orientation selectivity.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' conclusion based on their research.

claim: Otherwise, decoding would have suffered from shifting the slices by half the hypercolumn width.
source: Otherwise, decoding would have suffered from shifting the slices by half the hypercolumn width.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of fine-scale information.

claim: The current study characterizes one of the sources of the coarse-scale bias.
source: Rather than continuing to debate about whether fMRI decoding is dominated by coarse- or fine-scale information, the current study characterizes one of the sources of the coarse-scale bias, the implications of which are much broader than the technical details of orientation-decoding with fMRI (see above).
evidence: This is a statement of the contribution of the current study.

claim: The implications of the current study are much broader than the technical details of orientation-decoding with fMRI.
source: Rather than continuing to debate about whether fMRI decoding is dominated by coarse- or fine-scale information, the current study characterizes one of the sources of the coarse-scale bias, the implications of which are much broader than the technical details of orientation-decoding with fMRI (see above).
evidence: This is a statement of the significance of the current study.

claim: It is important to remember that the contribution of many decoding studies remains, irrespective of the source of decodable information.
source: Leaving aside this debate about whether orientation decoding with fMRI depends on coarse- vs. fine-scale information, it is important to remember that the contribution of many decoding studies remains, irrespective of the source of decodable information.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of prior research.

claim: A primary contribution of Kamitani and Tong (2005) regards feature-based attention: they showed that attending to one or the other orientation changes the activity in V1 in such a way that the attended orientation can be decoded.
source: For example, a primary contribution of Kamitani and Tong (2005) regards feature-based attention: they showed that attending to one or the other orientation changes the activity in V1 in such a way that the attended orientation can be decoded.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: That result holds regardless of whether the decoding depends on coarse- vs. fine-scale.
source: That result holds regardless of whether the decoding depends on coarse- vs. fine-scale.
evidence: This is an assertion about the interpretation of prior research.

claim: Haynes and Rees (2005) showed that V1 activity reflects properties of invisible stimuli, using decoding.
source: Similarly, Haynes and Rees (2005) showed that V1 activity reflects properties of invisible stimuli, using decoding.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: Most, if not all, of the findings from studies that used decoding, forward modeling, and other MVPA techniques do not depend on the source of decodable information.
source: Likewise for many studies that used decoding, forward modeling, and other MVPA techniques to reveal properties of cortical processing. Most, if not all, of these findings do not depend on the source of decodable information.
evidence: This is an assertion about the interpretation of prior research.

claim: Stimulus vignetting has previously been referred to as an 'edge effect'.
source: Stimulus vignetting has previously been referred to as an 'edge effect', and we demonstrated the intuition of stimulus vignetting using examples of hard edges (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about terminology and the presentation of the concept.

claim: Several studies have used gratings with smoothed edges.
source: Several studies have used gratings with smoothed edges, and some have smoothed the edges in an attempt to eliminate any effects related to the edge (Freeman et al., 2011; Warren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: According to the model, vignetting does not occur exclusively in the vicinity of edges.
source: According to the model, however, vignetting does not occur exclusively in the vicinity of edges.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: A contrast change, even a gradual change, is all that is necessary to produce stimulus vignetting.
source: Rather, a contrast change, even a gradual change, is all that is necessary to produce stimulus vignetting.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: The vignette causes the Fourier spectrum to splatter.
source: The vignette causes the Fourier spectrum to splatter (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Smoothing the stimulus edge only acts to spatially spread this effect across a larger portion of the visual field.
source: Smoothing the stimulus edge only acts to spatially spread this effect across a larger portion of the visual field.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: Both square-wave modulators and sinusoidal modulators evoked similar levels of vignetting.
source: Indeed, we found that both square-wave modulators and sinusoidal modulators evoked similar levels of vignetting, empirically confirming the model's prediction.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments.

claim: Other factors, in addition to stimulus vignetting, may contribute to the coarse-scale bias.
source: Other factors, in addition to stimulus vignetting, may contribute to the coarse-scale bias.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: The coarse-scale orientation bias may reflect, in addition to stimulus vignetting, a neuronal 'gain map'.
source: First, the coarse-scale orientation bias may reflect, in addition to stimulus vignetting, a neuronal 'gain map' (Philips and Chakravarthy, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: Neurons in visual cortex may have different response gains depending on their preferred orientations and receptive field locations.
source: Neurons in visual cortex may have different response gains depending on their preferred orientations and receptive field locations.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: A gain map could be instantiated in visual cortex through a number of different physiological mechanisms.
source: A gain map could be instantiated in visual cortex through a number of different physiological mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: The coarse-scale orientation bias might reflect 'asymmetric surround suppression', an imbalance in suppression between different parts of the region surrounding a neuron's receptive field.
source: Second, the coarse-scale orientation bias might reflect 'asymmetric surround suppression', an imbalance in suppression between different parts of the region surrounding a neuron's receptive field.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: The responsiveness of a V1 neuron is suppressed by stimuli outside its classical RF.
source: The responsiveness of a V1 neuron is suppressed by stimuli outside its classical RF (Sceniak et al., 1999; Sceniak et al., 2001; Cavanaugh et al., 2002a; Cavanaugh et al., 2002b; Zenger-Landolt and Heeger, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Suppression is stronger for neurons with RFs near the center of a stimulus aperture, less so for neurons with RFs near the aperture edge, because there is less stimulation surrounding those RFs.
source: Suppression is stronger for neurons with RFs near the center of a stimulus aperture, less so for neurons with RFs near the aperture edge, because there is less stimulation surrounding those RFs.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of surround suppression.

claim: For many neurons in V1, surround suppression is asymmetric, such that there is more suppression at the 'ends' of the receptive field (i.e., along the preferred orientation) than the 'sides'.
source: For many neurons in V1, surround suppression is asymmetric, such that there is more suppression at the 'ends' of the receptive field (i.e., along the preferred orientation) than the 'sides' (Larsson et al., 2017; Cavanaugh et al., 2002a; Cavanaugh et al., 2002b; Tanaka and Ohzawa, 2009; Hallum and Movshon, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Because of this asymmetry, the release from suppression may be greater for aperture edges that are orthogonal to each neuron's preferred orientation, such that a circular aperture centered at fixation will confer a radial bias.
source: Because of this asymmetry, the release from suppression may be greater for aperture edges that are orthogonal to each neuron's preferred orientation, such that a circular aperture centered at fixation will confer a radial bias.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of asymmetric surround suppression.

claim: Regardless of whether a gain map and/or asymmetric surround suppression contribute to coarse-scale orientation bias, stimulus vignetting shows a strong and robust effect on measured orientation preference.
source: Regardless of whether a gain map and/or asymmetric surround suppression contribute to coarse-scale orientation bias, stimulus vignetting shows a strong and robust effect on measured orientation preference.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The computations that give rise to orientation tuning in V1 remain inadequately understood.
source: Orientation is used as a model for understanding more complex feature processing in other cortical areas, and oriented V1-like receptive fields play an important role in successful computational models of vision. Yet, the computations that give rise to orientation tuning in V1 remain inadequately understood.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The results provide a framework for reinterpreting a wide-range of findings on orientation selectivity.
source: Our results provide a framework for reinterpreting a wide-range of findings on orientation selectivity.
evidence: This is a statement of the significance of the current study.

claim: The image-computable model is based on the steerable pyramid.
source: The image-computable model is based on the steerable pyramid (Simoncelli et al., 1992), a subband image transform that decomposes an image into orientation and spatial frequency channels (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the model, supported by a citation.

claim: The steerable pyramid is a subband image transform that decomposes an image into orientation and spatial frequency channels.
source: The image-computable model is based on the steerable pyramid (Simoncelli et al., 1992), a subband image transform that decomposes an image into orientation and spatial frequency channels (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the model, supported by a citation.

claim: The pyramid simulates the responses of a large number of linear receptive fields (RFs), each of which computes a weighted sum of the stimulus image.
source: The pyramid simulates the responses of a large number of linear receptive fields (RFs), each of which computes a weighted sum of the stimulus image; the weights determine the orientation and spatial frequency tuning.
evidence: This is a description of the model.

claim: RFs with the same orientation and spatial-frequency tuning, but shifted to different locations, are called a 'channel'.
source: RFs with the same orientation and spatial-frequency tuning, but shifted to different locations, are called a 'channel'.
evidence: This is a definition used in the model.

claim: The model used an instantiation with six orientations, which resulted in a bandwidth comparable to empirical tuning curves measured in primate electrophysiological recordings.
source: We used an instantiation of the model with six orientations, which resulted in a bandwidth comparable to empirical tuning curves measured in primate electrophysiological recordings (Ringach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters, supported by a citation.

claim: Using four or more bands with correspondingly broader or narrower tuning curves yielded similar results supporting the same conclusions.
source: Using four or more bands with correspondingly broader or narrower tuning curves yielded similar results supporting the same conclusions.
evidence: This is a description of the robustness of the model results.

claim: The number of spatial frequency channels was determined by the size of the input images and the spatial frequency bandwidth.
source: The number of spatial frequency channels was determined by the size of the input images and the spatial frequency bandwidth.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: Images were 768 × 1024 pixels, and a spatial frequency bandwidth of 0.5 octaves was used, resulting in 15 different spatial frequency channels.
source: We used images that were 768 × 1024 pixels, and a spatial frequency bandwidth of 0.5 octaves, and so the model had 15 different spatial frequency channels.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: The RFs cover all orientations and spatial frequencies evenly.
source: The RFs cover all orientations and spatial frequencies evenly (i.e., the sum of the squares of the tuning curves is exactly equal to one for all orientations and spatial frequencies).
evidence: This is a description of the model properties.

claim: For each orientation and spatial frequency, the pyramid includes RFs with two different phases, analogous to odd- and even-phase Gabor filters.
source: For each orientation and spatial frequency, the pyramid includes RFs with two different phases, analogous to odd- and even-phase Gabor filters.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The sum of the squares of the responses of two such RFs computes what has been called an 'energy' response.
source: The sum of the squares of the responses of two such RFs computes what has been called an 'energy' response (Adelson and Bergen, 1985; Heeger, 1992) because it depends on the local spectral energy within a spatial region of the stimulus, for a particular orientation and spatial frequency.
evidence: This is a description of the model computation, supported by citations.

claim: The linear RFs in the model are hypothesized to be a basis set of orientation and spatial frequency tuning curves of V1 neurons.
source: The linear RFs in the model are hypothesized to be a basis set of orientation and spatial frequency tuning curves of V1 neurons; any invertible linear transform of the basis set can be substituted (Freeman and Adelson, 1991; Simoncelli et al., 1992; Simoncelli, 1993) and different such transforms can be substituted at each spatial location, consistent with the diversity in the tuning properties of V1 neurons, without changing the nature of the representation.
evidence: This is a description of the model's theoretical basis, supported by citations.

claim: The model was designed so that the filters evenly tile retinotopic space, orientation, and spatial frequency to avoid any possibility of the kind of artifact that was suggested to underlie Carlson (2014) simulation results.
source: The model was designed so that the filters evenly tile retinotopic space, orientation, and spatial frequency to avoid any possibility of the kind of artifact that was suggested to underlie Carlson (2014) simulation results (Clifford and Mannion, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the model design rationale, supported by citations.

claim: The strength of the model is its simplicity.
source: The strength of the model is its simplicity.
evidence: This is a statement about the model design philosophy.

claim: The goal is not to provide an accurate model of V1 activity, but rather to provide a platform for assessing vignetting.
source: Our goal is not to provide an accurate model of V1 activity, but rather to provide a platform for assessing vignetting.
evidence: This is a statement about the model design philosophy.

claim: The authors purposely kept the model simple so that they could be certain that vignetting is indeed the source of orientation bias in the model.
source: We purposely kept the model simple so that we could be certain that vignetting is indeed the source of orientation bias in the model.
evidence: This is a statement about the model design philosophy.

claim: Thirteen observers (eight females, aged 22–27 years) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in the study.
source: Thirteen observers (eight females, aged 22–27 years) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in the study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Observers provided written informed consent.
source: Observers provided written informed consent.
evidence: This is a description of the ethical procedures.

claim: The consent and experimental protocol were in compliance with the safety guidelines for MRI research, and were approved by both the University Committee on Activities involving Human Subjects at New York University, and the Institutional Review Board at National Institutes of Health.
source: The consent and experimental protocol were in compliance with the safety guidelines for MRI research, and were approved by both the University Committee on Activities involving Human Subjects at New York University, and the Institutional Review Board at National Institutes of Health.
evidence: This is a description of the ethical procedures.
